materials.transcript: Today we will examine how researchers evaluate rain gardens in urban neighbourhoods. These are shallow planted areas that receive runoff from nearby hard surfaces. Their main purpose is not simply to store water in a visible pond. Instead, they encourage infiltration, which means movement of water into the ground. This distinction matters because a garden that looks dry may already have processed a substantial amount of rainfall. Before construction, our fictional research team compared several sites. A sandy soil allowed water to pass through rapidly, whereas a layer of clay slowed it down. The team selected a site with that slower layer so they could investigate a practical difficulty rather than demonstrate an ideal case. They also recorded the depth of the soil, since performance depends on more than the material found at the surface. The design requirement was that standing water should disappear within forty-eight hours after an ordinary storm. This limit was chosen to protect the plants and keep the space usable. It was not a promise that the garden could absorb any storm, however intense. During exceptional rainfall, an overflow channel would carry excess water safely towards the existing drainage system instead of allowing it to enter neighbouring buildings. To estimate the amount of water entering the garden, the students first measured the area of the roof connected to its inlet pipe. They deliberately excluded a nearby car park because its runoff went to a separate drain. A rain gauge provided the depth of each storm. Combining that measurement with the connected area gave an approximate incoming volume, although small losses still had to be acknowledged. A second garden was needed for comparison. The students matched its size and planting pattern as closely as possible to the first. They also checked local traffic, since pollution washed from busy roads could influence water quality independently of the planting. Without this precaution, a difference in the samples might have been attributed to the gardens when it actually reflected the surrounding neighbourhoods. Continuous measurements were collected by sensors positioned at the inlet and near the bottom of the planted basin. The instruments were checked against manual readings every week, because a smooth electronic record is not necessarily an accurate one. When a battery failed, the gap was marked as missing data. The researchers did not quietly substitute an average and present it as something they had directly observed. One unexpected difficulty emerged after several months. A deposit of sediment had formed close to the inlet, reducing the rate at which water could enter the planting bed. Removing it improved drainage, but the team recorded the labour involved. A system that works only when someone cleans it every few days may be less attractive to a local authority than its initial construction cost suggests. The study also considered biodiversity. Volunteers counted the different kinds of insects visiting the plants, using the same observation period at both sites. These counts were kept separate from the drainage results. More insect visitors did not prove that less water reached the sewer, just as rapid drainage did not prove that the site supported a wide range of wildlife. Each outcome required its own evidence. Residents could contribute observations, but photographs alone were not sufficient for measuring water depth. The volunteers received a short training session and used a marked measuring stick at a fixed location. Their reports were then compared with the instrument records. This arrangement made participation useful without pretending that every contribution had the same precision, and it helped the students identify unusual events worth investigating. Finally, the team considered whether the design could be used elsewhere. They calculated costs over several years, including replacement plants, cleaning and routine maintenance. The recommendation was conditional: similar gardens might be appropriate where soil, rainfall and available staff were comparable. The project therefore offered a method for making a decision, rather than a claim that one small installation had solved flooding across an entire city.

materials.passage: City authorities increasingly plant trees to reduce uncomfortable summer heat. Yet a photograph of a leafy street cannot reveal how much protection its residents receive. Surface temperature, air temperature and the heat experienced by a person are related but different measurements. A pavement can become much cooler in shade while the surrounding air changes relatively little. Evaluating a planting programme therefore requires a clear question: is the aim to protect pedestrians during a short journey, reduce heat inside buildings, or change conditions across a neighbourhood? The answer determines which observations will be useful, and which attractive numbers may be misleading. Consider a fictional study in the city of Bellhaven. Researchers placed instruments on two streets with similar building heights and road widths. One had mature trees; the other had few. Measurements were taken at the same height and at matching times, rather than whenever a member of the team happened to visit. This design reduced some obvious sources of variation, but it did not turn the streets into identical environments. Traffic, the materials used on walls and the direction of the afternoon sun could still influence the readings. The team therefore described the comparison as evidence of an association, not a controlled experiment proving a single cause. The strongest immediate benefit came from blocking direct sunlight. Tree canopies intercepted radiation before it reached people and paving. A second process involved water: leaves released moisture, and evaporation used energy that would otherwise have contributed to heating. However, the importance of this process depended on access to water. A thirsty tree could close the tiny openings in its leaves, reducing moisture loss and limiting this cooling effect. Species selection consequently involved a compromise between survival during dry periods and the amount of water available for cooling. Simply counting trees said little about how these mechanisms operated. Where trees were located also mattered. A broad canopy above a quiet parking area might lower a satellite image's average surface temperature while offering little help to people waiting for a bus. The Bellhaven researchers mapped walking routes, crossings and places where passengers stood without cover. They then considered the time of day when each place was used. This approach shifted attention from the total area of green cover to the relationship between shade and human activity. It also exposed a practical constraint: underground pipes sometimes prevented planting at exactly the locations where new shade would be most valuable. Benefits were not distributed evenly. Residents in rented flats often had less control over nearby planting than owners of large gardens. Older people and outdoor workers could face greater exposure even when the average temperature of their district appeared moderate. The research team therefore invited community groups to identify overlooked locations. Their accounts did not replace temperature measurements; they helped explain which measurements should be collected. A shaded route to a clinic, for example, could be important despite serving fewer people than a central shopping street. Deciding between such projects required an explicit judgement about public priorities. Long-term planning introduced further uncertainty. Young trees provided limited shade, and some failed before reaching maturity. Maintenance, including watering and protecting roots during road repairs, affected the eventual outcome. In the fictional study, the council compared immediate expenditure with the expected cost of care over twenty years. It did not assume that every planted tree would survive for that entire period. The researchers also warned against using one unusually cool summer as proof of permanent success. Monitoring needed to cover different weather conditions, while the original measurement method had to remain consistent enough for comparisons to retain meaning. The study's conclusion was deliberately cautious. Trees could be a valuable component of heat adaptation, but they could not replace every other measure. Shelters might provide shade before a canopy developed, and improvements to buildings could reduce exposure indoors. A useful assessment would combine evidence about physical conditions, the needs of vulnerable residents and the resources available for continued care. Rather than asking whether trees were universally effective, decision makers were encouraged to ask where particular designs would work, who would benefit and what would be required to sustain those benefits. That narrower question produced a more practical and transparent basis for local action.

materials.prompt: Some people believe that cities should spend more money on public transport than on new roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
selfCheck: 立场是否明确，主体段是否解释理由和具体例子？
是否回应public transport与new roads的资金比较？
是否在讨论限制条件后仍保持结论一致？
按任务回应、连贯衔接、词汇、语法四维自查；保存首稿与修改稿。
materials.example:
I largely agree that cities should give public transport a higher funding priority than new roads. Reliable buses and trains can move many people through a limited space, while additional road capacity may provide only temporary relief. Nevertheless, some road investment remains necessary for safety and access.

The strongest reason to favour public transport is that urban space cannot expand as quickly as demand for travel. A frequent bus service can carry passengers who would otherwise use separate cars. If it connects residential areas with workplaces and operates beyond office hours, it becomes a practical choice for a wider group of residents. For example, a worker finishing late may leave the car at home when the last bus is predictable. Investment should therefore improve frequency and reliability, rather than merely produce an impressive new station.

There is also an issue of access. People who cannot drive still need to reach schools, hospitals and jobs. Spending most of a transport budget on roads may improve journeys for motorists while doing little for these residents. Affordable fares and accessible vehicles can make public expenditure useful to more of the population. This does not mean that every route must attract identical passenger numbers; some provide an essential connection for smaller communities.

However, prioritising public transport should not imply neglecting roads altogether. Dangerous junctions need repair, and emergency services require dependable access. In rapidly growing districts, a carefully planned road connection may also be necessary. Such projects should be assessed against clear needs instead of an assumption that more traffic always requires more lanes.

Overall, cities should direct the larger share of new transport funding towards dependable public services, while maintaining roads and addressing specific safety problems. This balance recognises both the limitations of urban space and the different needs of residents.

materials.prompt: The table shows the percentage of commuters using three main forms of transport in the fictional city of Bellhaven in 2005, 2015 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

taskData.description: 虚构数据：每年三种主要通勤方式的占比，单位为%。

selfCheck: 是否给出清楚总览，而不是逐格罗列？
数字和年份是否准确，percentage points是否与percentage区分？
是否比较三种方式，避免编造表外原因？
按任务完成、连贯衔接、词汇、语法四维自查。
materials.example:
The table compares the proportions of commuters travelling by car, bus and bicycle in Bellhaven in three selected years between 2005 and 2025.

Overall, bus travel became increasingly common and replaced cars as the largest category. Cycling also gained a greater share, although it remained the least frequently used of the three forms of transport throughout the period.

In 2005, half of commuters used a car, while buses accounted for 40 percent. The remaining 10 percent travelled by bicycle. Ten years later, the car figure had fallen to 40 percent. By contrast, the proportion taking a bus rose to 45 percent, putting it five percentage points above the car category. The bicycle share also increased, reaching 15 percent in 2015.

The changes continued in the final year shown. Bus use reached 55 percent in 2025, compared with 25 percent for cars and 20 percent for bicycles. Over the whole period, the car share declined by 25 percentage points, whereas the bus and bicycle figures increased by 15 and 10 points respectively. The table provides no information about the reasons behind these changes.

materials.example:
A useful skill I learned was organising information in a spreadsheet. I started learning it about two years ago, when my team needed to compare several weeks of work records. At first I copied numbers manually and made quite a few mistakes, so I realised that I needed a more consistent method.

A colleague showed me how to put each type of information in its own column and use simple formulas. What helped most was practising with a small set of real records rather than watching a long tutorial from beginning to end. When something went wrong, I could see exactly which result looked unreasonable and ask a specific question.

The skill has been useful because I can now check a pattern before discussing it with other people. For example, if a task seems to take longer on certain days, I can compare the records instead of relying entirely on memory. I still check the original information, because a spreadsheet cannot make inaccurate data reliable.

I would not describe myself as an expert. There are many advanced features I have never used. However, being able to organise a simple table has saved time and made my explanations clearer. It also taught me that learning a small, practical skill well can be more valuable than collecting a large number of techniques I never apply.

prompts: Why do some adults find it difficult to learn new skills?
Should employers pay for staff training?
How can technology help people learn, and what are its limitations?
Is practical experience more valuable than formal education?
reviewChecklist: 先录首答，再看示例；回听原录音并保留修订前后两份。
检查流利与连贯、词汇、语法、发音；ASR转写与时长不能替代真人评分。
materials.example:
One difficulty for adults is that learning competes with work and family responsibilities. A short course may be easier to maintain than a demanding programme, but it still needs a clear purpose. People are more likely to continue when they can use the new skill soon afterwards.

I think employers should fund training when it is directly connected with a person's role. Both sides can benefit: the employee develops useful knowledge, and the organisation gains a more capable team. However, the training should include time to practise. Paying for a course without allowing anyone to apply it is unlikely to achieve much.

Technology can make explanations available at a convenient time and provide opportunities for repeated practice. It is particularly helpful when learners need to review a difficult step. Its limitation is that an automatic system may not understand why an answer was produced. Feedback from a knowledgeable person can reveal a mistaken assumption that a simple score misses.

Practical experience and formal education serve different purposes. Experience shows how ideas behave under real constraints, while education can provide concepts for understanding unfamiliar situations. Someone who has only experience may repeat a method without knowing its limits; someone with only theory may underestimate practical difficulties. I would therefore prefer a system that connects both, with learners explaining their decisions and then testing them in realistic tasks. These are separate discussion examples, not a script to memorise.
